subject: Electrical Engineering
title: Induction Motors: No Magnets Needed
description: A 60-second lesson on Induction Motors: No Magnets Needed.

hook.text: The induction motor has no permanent magnets and no electrical connection to the rotor.

buildup.text: AC in the stator creates a rotating magnetic field that sweeps around the motor.

discovery.text: The rotating field induces current in the rotor's conductors, which creates its own field and torque.

twist.text: The rotor must slip behind the field's speed — if it catches up, induction stops and torque vanishes.

climax.text: Induction motors run about half of all electric motors worldwide — robust and inexpensive.

punchline.text: No contact, no magnets — just fields inducing fields, spinning on their own.

quiz.question: Why must the rotor of an induction motor 'slip' behind the rotating field?
options: Bearings create friction that limits rotor speed
If the rotor matches field speed, no relative motion means no induction and no torque
The stator windings limit the maximum rotor speed
